summary: A 1975 slight revision of RFC 686, on the subject of print files in FTP. It is part of a long discussion that includes RFC 640, RFC 630, RFC 542, RFC 454, RFC 448, RFC 414, RFC 385 and RFC 354.

eli5.summary: This is a small fix to an earlier note about sending files meant for printers over the network.

questions: one more try on the ftp
what is the ftp srvr command
what did rfc 691 change from rfc 686
subtitle: A revised plea to fix FTP-1's rough edges, with a new approach to print files using the SRVR command.

tldr.problem: Hosts ran the first version of FTP but disagreed on print files, HELP and STAT replies, and error codes, while FTP-2 existed only on paper.
tldr.mechanism: This slight revision of RFC 686 argues for fixing FTP-1 in place: recipient-side print handling, receiver-only details carried by the SRVR command, a 200 reply to end HELP, and temporary versus permanent errors split between 4xx and 5xx.
tldr.outcome: The author proposes that, absent objections before June 1, everyone treat the changes as official, though he admits they are not necessarily the best possible and only easily doable.

today: RFC 691 revises RFC 686 and is dated June 1975; the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown and shows no later RFC replacing it. It captures one participant's proposals in a 1975 FTP debate.

sections.title: A Revision of RFC 686
sections.content:
RFC 691 is a slight revision of RFC 686, mainly different in its handling of print files. After reading several RFCs he had not known about, Brian Harvey says he was right all along but for the wrong reasons. The list of reply codes is also adjusted to reflect the four earlier lists (RFCs 354, 454, 542 and 640) more fully.

He suggests that if no one objects before June 1, everyone take it as official that HELP returns 200, that SRVR is used as described, and that "permanent" 4xx errors become 5xx. He stresses the changes are not necessarily the best possible, only easily doable.
sections.eli5: He rewrote his earlier note, mostly the part about printer files, and asked for objections by a set date.

sections.title: Print Files and the SRVR Command
sections.content:
The data sent for an ASCII or EBCDIC print file should contain Fortran control characters and be sent as is; the recipient reformats it, not the server. He notes the latest FTP-1 document on the subject (RFC 454) invents a FORM command, while FTP-2 puts the format in the TYPE command; neither conveys more than the existing A-P-E-F scheme.

FTP-2 also adds a Telnet-formatted versus non-print distinction. He argues hosts should not have to negotiate something that does not change what goes over the net. Instead, information that affects only the recipient should go in a form the sender can ignore: the SRVR command. His examples: TYPE A, DISP PRINT, RETR FOO to retrieve, and TYPE A, SRVR PRINT, STOR FOO to send.

Registered SRVR parameters are T (Telnet print file) and N (normal, which turns off any earlier SRVR). Parameters may be longer than one letter, and an initial X marks local idiosyncrasies.
sections.eli5: Printer instructions only matter to whoever receives the file, so he says to pass them as a side note the sender can simply forward without understanding.

sections.title: Reply Code Problems and Fixes
sections.content:
As in RFC 686, a user program can read replies by their first digit: 0 or 1 shown and ignored, 2 success, 4 or 5 failure, and 3 only for the 300 greeting, 330 password request and 350 mail response. The trouble is HELP, which returns 0xx, 1xx or 2xx depending on the server, while STAT replies use 151 lines ending in 200 END OF STATUS. He notes RFC 414 approves a 200 reply for both STAT and HELP, and asks that all servers end HELP with 200.

He also dislikes 9xx experimental codes (sanctioned by RFC 385) because a program cannot tell if they are positive or negative, and proposes experimental replies inside 000-599 using x9x or xx9. Following RFC 630 and RFC 640, he suggests 4xx for temporary and 5xx for permanent failures, so mailers can decide whether to retry.
sections.eli5: Replies are number codes. He wants help text to end with a clear "done" code, experiments to use numbers programs can still understand, and temporary and lasting errors to be told apart.

sections.title: Why Not Wait for FTP-2
sections.content:
The rest of the RFC repeats RFC 686's points against FTP-2: TELNET-2 echo negotiation is pointless for programs, the committee origin is no reason, default data sockets are a security matter, being online is no argument, and MODE and STRU changes can be handled inside FTP-1, as the TENEX paged-file work (RFC 683) shows. He is happy with transfers as they are and thinks FTP-2's existence is mainly an excuse for not solving FTP-1 problems.

It ends with a renumbering of the current FTP-1 reply codes.
sections.eli5: He ends by saying the old tool mostly works, and a new version should not be an excuse to skip fixing it.
